title: QNTN: Establishing a Regional Quantum Network in Tennessee
problem: Design and compare architectural approaches for interconnecting three quantum local area networks across different cities using satellite constellations or high-altitude platforms to distribute quantum entanglement across a region.
motivation: Regional quantum networks require optimal architectural design to enable practical scaling of quantum computing infrastructure across multiple distributed facilities.
method: The paper compares two interconnection architectures: a space-ground approach deploying 108 satellites, and an air-ground approach using high-altitude platforms (HAPs). Both are evaluated for geographic coverage, entanglement distribution request fulfillment rate, and quantum fidelity metrics.
key_novelty: Systematic quantitative comparison of satellite constellation versus HAP-based architectures for regional quantum network interconnection with explicit coverage, reliability, and fidelity trade-offs.
contributions: Performance evaluation of 108-satellite constellation for regional quantum entanglement distribution
Analysis of HAP-based air-ground architecture achieving full-day coverage and 100% request fulfillment
Quantified trade-offs between architectures: 55.17% vs full coverage, 57.75% vs 100% request fulfillment, 0.96 vs 0.98 fidelity
Identification of HAP operational challenges including limited uptime, vibration sensitivity, weather dependency, and maintenance requirements

metrics.other: coverage (55.17% satellite vs full-day HAP), request_fulfillment (57.75% satellite vs 100% HAP), fidelity (0.96 satellite vs 0.98 HAP)

limitations: Does not discuss cost analysis, power consumption, or scalability beyond regional scope; HAP operational limitations are identified but not quantitatively compared with satellite deployment complexity.
